chapter_theme: Short poems of the five lands in many voices: the woman desolate when he goes (41, 43, 46, 50, 54), the friend testing or holding the man to his word (42, 47, 53, 55), the foster mother on the eloped girl's trail (44), vows that reach past death and birth (49, 57), the consent of kin and gossip (51), the lover's sickness his friends cannot cure (58), and the pleasure of merely seeing him (60).

41.reading: The woman tells her friend that while her lover is near she delights like a town holding its festival, but since he went away she is desolate and dull, like an empty house in a little hamlet by the wasteland whose people have left and in whose yard squirrels play.
41.nuance: Both similes are places, a crowded festival town and an emptied yard; the squirrels playing freely in the yard are the sign that no one is left, so her emptiness is measured by what now moves in it. The poet is named after line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of the time after he has gone away

comparisons.tenor: her delight while he is near, like a town in festival
her dull desolation since he left

42.reading: The friend asks the man of the hill land, where after the cloud-massed rain falls at midnight the waterfall goes on sounding in the clefts, whether, even if desire should end, our bond with him could ever wane.
42.nuance: The friend grants that kaamam may end and asks only whether the bond will; தேயுமோ, 'will it wane', is the moon's verb. The image sits in the address to him, where the hill lord's own land answers her question before he can.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill clefts, the waterfall and midnight

ullurai.tenor: desire and the bond that should outlast it

pairs.situation: desire, which comes down in one burst and is spent
the bond, which should go on sounding after the desire has passed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the rain and waterfall of the hero's own hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

43.reading: The woman says she made light of it, thinking he would not go, and he made light of it, thinking she would not bear it; caught in the clash their two great prides made, her troubled heart writhes as if a cobra had seized it.
43.nuance: Avvaiyar gives the same verb to both (இகழ்ந்தனனே, இகழ்ந்தனரே) and calls the silence of both ஆண்மை, a word of manly pride, used here of the woman too: each was sure of the other, neither spoke, and the parting happened between them. The poem does not say what the snake seizes; the moon in eclipse is one reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going away, which neither spoke of

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

44.reading: The foster mother, following the girl who has gone off with her lover, says her legs are worn out and her eyes have lost their light from looking and looking, and that the others in this world, none of them her girl, are surely more than the stars of the wide dark sky.
44.nuance: The poem never says whom she seeks; the speaker and the eyes that have lost their light from looking make it the search. பிறரே, 'others', is the last word: everyone she has looked at is someone else.

thinai_evidence.note: the search on the road for the girl who has gone with her lover

comparisons.tenor: the strangers she has looked at in her search

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee in the poem; she speaks to herself on the road

45.reading: The friend says that the lord of the rich town rose at dawn, yoked his swift chariot and went to embrace women of bright jewels, and when he stays out long the mother of his little son grieves; how searing it is, she says, to be born into this station.
45.nuance: திணை here is birth or station, not landscape: what burns is being born to a family whose wife must keep the house while the man goes to other women. The friend names the wife only as the mother of the little son, the title that binds her to stay. எல்லினன் is taken as 'he is late'.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the rich town goes to other women and his wife grieves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: he is spoken of in the third person, so the friend answers someone sent by him

46.reading: The woman asks her friend whether, in the land where he has gone, there is no grieving, lonely evening like this one, when the house sparrows with folded wings the colour of water-lily ash, having eaten the grain drying in the yard and bathed in the fine dust of the dung in the common ground, settle with their young in the nest under the eaves.
46.nuance: The colophon's thinai is marutham, the land of the village yard the sparrows live in; the situation, a man gone to another land and a woman alone at evening, is paalai's. The question is whether evening exists where he is: if it did, he would feel what she feels and come.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to another land and she bears the evening alone

iraicchi.act: the sparrows come back at evening to the nest in the eaves and stay there with their young
iraicchi.sense: even the house sparrow is home with its young at nightfall, while he stays away in another land

47.reading: The friend tells the long white moon that, in the forest where the boulder strewn with the falling blossoms of the black-trunked vengai looks like a great tiger's cub, it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
47.nuance: The moon does two harms at once: its light shows the lovers to watchers, and it makes the rock under the vengai look like a tiger, so the night path is both seen and fearful. The man is not addressed; he is meant to understand that the night meetings cannot go on. The poet is named after line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and the tiger of the hill forest

comparisons.tenor: the boulder spotted with fallen vengai blossoms

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the moon; by the usual reading the man, standing by, is meant to hear

48.reading: The friend asks whether the lover will not send even one word of the kind she longs for, to clear the pallor from her fair forehead, though she suffers greatly in this way even after hearing her playmates at the oorai game tell her to beware the grief of the morning, when the cool dew-wet doll they made of pollen will wilt.
48.nuance: The playmates' warning about the pollen doll that wilts by morning reads as said of her: her beauty is as perishable as the toy. இன்ன பண்பின், 'of such a nature', joins the two, but the construction of lines 1 to 4 is not certain. One kind word is all the friend asks of him.

thinai_evidence.note: her pallor while the lover is away and sends no word

comparisons.tenor: the girl's beauty, which wilts as she grieves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: unclear: she speaks of the girl and of the lover in the third person

49.reading: The woman tells the lord of the shore of dark sapphire waters, where the water-thorn's blossoms with ripe pollen are like a squirrel's teeth, that even when this life turns into the next, may he be her husband and may she be the one close to his heart.
49.nuance: The vow stretches the marriage past this life and asks for two things, not one: that he be her husband, and that she be the one his heart agrees with (நெஞ்சு நேர்பவள்). The second wish admits a doubt the first does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-thorn and the lord of the strand; the situation is a vow, not a lament

comparisons.tenor: the water-thorn's blossoms with ripe pollen
the dark great waters of the shore

50.reading: The woman says the ford of his town is adorned with small nyaazhal blossoms like mustard seeds strewn with the spent flowers of the fresh marutham, while the shoulders he embraced, wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, are adorned with loneliness.
50.nuance: The same verb closes both halves: அணிந்தன்று, 'is adorned', for his ford and for her shoulders. His place wears flowers and hers wears loneliness; the parallel is the reproach. The colophon says marutham; the uri of lament, with the shore tree nyaazhal, points to neythal.

thinai_evidence.note: her lament as her body wastes is irangal, though the ford mixes neythal and marutham trees

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

51.reading: The friend says that the lord of the shore of pure sand, where the cold dewy flowers of the bent-thorned water-thorn, blown by the wind like pearls from a broken string, spread over every ford, is loved by her too; their mother is very fond of him, their father wants to give the girl to him, and the gossiping town too speaks her name with his.
51.nuance: Each one who might stand in the way is turned in his favour: the friend, the mother, the father and at last the town, whose அம்பல் usually threatens secret love and here pairs the girl with him. யானும் காதலென், 'I too love him', is the friend speaking as one with the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-thorn on the sands and the lord of the strand

comparisons.tenor: the water-thorn blossoms scattered by the wind

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the man is spoken of in the third person

52.reading: The friend tells the girl with thick dark hair smelling of naranda and rows of bright white teeth that when she saw her trembling, like one desired by the spirit of the water-bright slope trampled by the feeding elephant, she felt for her, little by little, did she not?
52.nuance: சூர் நசைந்தனையை, 'like one the spirit has desired', is how a girl's lovesickness looks to those who do not know its cause; the friend says she saw it and understood. Whether பரிந்தனென் is pity for the girl or a plea made on her behalf is not settled by the verse.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant, the hill slope and its spirit

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the girl named in lines 3-4 is taken as the one addressed

53.reading: The friend tells the man of the fields that what afflicts us is the oath he swore at the broad ford of our town, holding the girl's forearm with the hill-goddesses as witness, by the sand dune where the yard's punku blossoms lie on the white sand like the bright puffed red rice the velan scatters on every ground of his possession rite.
53.nuance: அணங்கு is turned round: what afflicts them is not the goddess but the oath sworn before the goddesses, which will punish its breaker and, the friend fears, those he swore to. The velan's scattered rice brings the possession rite into the scene, as if the ground of the oath were already a ground of veri.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend holds the man of the fields to the oath he has broken

comparisons.tenor: the punku blossoms fallen on the white sand

54.reading: The woman says she is here, but her beauty has stayed there with the man of the forest land, where the green bamboo the forest elephant lets go, frightened by the sling-noise of the millet-field watchmen, springs up like a rod that has struck a fish.
54.nuance: Line 1 splits her in two, I am here and my beauty is there, so nalam becomes a thing that can leave with him. The poet is named after the simile of line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, its watchmen and the forest elephant

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo springing up when the elephant lets go

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

ullurai.tenor: the man who lets her go for fear of the watch kept on her

pairs.situation: the watch and talk that frighten him off
he lets go of her, who is left behind
she is left shaken, her beauty gone with him

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the millet field she herself guards and the elephant of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

55.reading: The friend says that as the sapphire flowers of the great backwater close, and the stroking cold wind comes bringing mist with the spray of the white waves to leave us helpless, this small good town has become, for these few days, a painful place to live.
55.nuance: The closing flowers mark the evening without naming it. The town is called small and good (சிறுநல்லூர்) and painful in one breath: the place has not changed, only the season and his absence have.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the waves and the cold wind at nightfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the complaint is meant to make him hasten

56.reading: The man on the waterless road says: let her of the bangled hands come and drink with me this little rotten water swarmed by wasps, left over when the hunting wild dogs dug and drank; she is to be pitied, pitied, she who dwells in my heart.
56.nuance: The wish holds two readings: he would have her share even this water, so that love would make it sweet, or he pictures her drinking it and pities her for it; அளியளோ அளியள் keeps both. கிளைத்து, 'dug', can also mean 'with their kin', which would make the dogs a pack sharing the water as he would share it with her; that reading is too doubtful to tag.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunting wild dogs and the fouled water of the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks of her to himself

57.reading: The woman wishes that, with a love that never slackens and cannot bear parting, like the union of the water-dwelling makanril pair for whom even a flower slipping between them seems a year gone by, their two lives might go out together, so that in this world where they live as two who know their duty they may escape the misery of one being left alone.
57.nuance: கடனறிந்து இருவேம் ஆகிய, 'we two who live knowing our duty', places the wish inside married life: the fear is not of a journey but of one death before the other.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of parting and of being left alone is lament

comparisons.tenor: a flower's moment between the birds, felt as a year
their love that cannot bear parting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from நாம் and இருவேம், which include him

58.reading: The man tells the friends who rebuke him that it would be well indeed if they could hold back this sickness for his sake, but it has spread like butter melting on a sun-scorched rock, watched over by a handless mute with only his eyes, and it is hard to bear.
58.nuance: The image stacks three helplessnesses: the keeper has no hands to gather the butter, no voice to call for help, and only his eyes to watch it melt. The rebukers are granted their good intent; the reply is that rebuke cannot reach what has already spread.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's love-sickness in secret love, which his friends rebuke

comparisons.vehicle: கையில் ஊமன் கண்ணிற் காக்கும் வெண்ணெய் உணங்கல் போலப்

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companions who rebuke him (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்)

59.reading: The friend asks whether he could forget her fragrant forehead, which smells of wild jasmine bundled with blue water-lilies from the deep wide-mouthed spring of Athalai hill, ruled by the lord of the gift-seekers who beat the pathalai drum; and since rare wealth beyond many wastelands is never filled up however one strives, she says, he will not stay long.
59.nuance: The comfort has two arguments: he cannot forget her, since the scent of a named hill's flowers is the memory he carries, and wealth is never complete, so there is no point in his staying to complete it. The second turns the reason for his journey against its length.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the wastelands in search of wealth

60.reading: The woman says that, like a dark-legged cripple who sees a great honeycomb on the high cliff where short-stemmed koothali sways and, sitting below, cups his palm into a little bowl, points and licks it, even if her lover does not grace her or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
60.nuance: The cripple never tastes the honey: he points at it and licks his empty cupped hand, so the simile makes the sweetness of seeing him an imagined taste. நல்கார் நயவார் ஆயினும் concedes the worst before claiming the sweetness.

thinai_evidence.note: the koothali and the honeycomb of the high cliff

comparisons.vehicle: முடவன் உட்கைச் சிறுகுடை கோலிக் கீழிருந்து சுட்டுபு நக்கி
comparisons.tenor: her pleasure in merely seeing him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

links.note: Naladiyar 125 says the bond (தொடர்பு) with small men wanes (தேயுமே) of itself like the moon while friendship with the great grows; Kuruntokai 42 asks the hill lord whether our bond (எம் தொடர்பும்) will wane (தேயுமோ) even if desire ends.
links.teaches: The same two words, bond and waning, show the friend putting the lover to the Naladiyar's test of character: a bond that wanes once its first cause, desire, is spent marks the small man, so her question demands that he prove himself one of the great.

links.note: Kural 1151 has the woman (or her friend) speak at once: if you are not leaving, tell me; your quick return, tell those who will still be alive. Kuruntokai 43 says neither spoke: she thought he would not go, he thought she would not bear it.
links.teaches: The couplet is the sentence whose absence Avvaiyar's poem mourns: set beside it, the poem shows a parting that happened because pride on both sides kept that sentence unsaid, so the Kural's bluntness reads as the cure for the silence that undid the Kuruntokai pair.

links.note: In Akananuru 7 the foster mother, following her eloped daughter into the waste, cannot catch up and questions a hill girl she meets; in Kuruntokai 44 her legs are worn out, her eyes dimmed from looking, and the others she sees are more than the stars.
links.teaches: Together they give the search its course: the long poem is its middle, where the nurse still questions each stranger in hope, and the four-line poem is its end, where every face has proved to be someone else's and the looking itself has cost her sight.

links.note: Kural 1222: the woman tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard-eyed as hers. Kuruntokai 46 asks whether the sad evening (புன்கண் மாலை) is absent in the land where he has gone.
links.teaches: Both women make the evening's sorrow a test of the absent man: the couplet asks whether the evening's partner is as hard as hers, the poem asks whether he has any evening at all, and its sparrows settling with their young supply what the couplet leaves out, that evening is when every creature with a home returns to it.

links.note: Kural 1119: the man tells the moon that if it would resemble her face it must not appear for many to see. Kuruntokai 47: the friend tells the long white moon it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
links.teaches: Both speakers wish the moon would not shine for others, for opposite reasons: the Kural's lover wants her face kept to himself, the Kuruntokai friend wants the meeting kept from watchers, so the moon's openness, which the couplet turns into a compliment, is in the older poem the danger that ends secret love.

links.note: Kural 1315: the man says they will not part in this birth, and her eyes fill with tears. Kuruntokai 49: the woman asks that even when this life turns into the next he be her husband.
links.teaches: The couplet's joke rests on a wish it never states, that the bond reach past this birth; Kuruntokai 49 is that wish in the woman's own mouth, so the pair shows why 'in this birth' wounds her: she had asked for the next one too.

links.note: Kural 1234: with her partner gone, her shoulders have lost their old beauty and fullness and her bright bangles slip. Kuruntokai 50: the shoulders he embraced have wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, adorned with loneliness.
links.teaches: The couplet names the wasted shoulder and slipping bangle as the sign of separation; the poem shows what the sign was used to say, setting it against his town's ford adorned with flowers, so the body's loss becomes an accusation of a place that still flourishes.

links.note: Kural 1143: the man asks whether the gossip the town knows is not welcome, since it is like having what he has not yet obtained. Kuruntokai 51: the friend says the gossiping town too speaks of the girl with him, and her mother and father favour him.
links.teaches: The couplet values gossip as a foretaste of a union not yet had; the poem shows the next step, when talk that pairs the lovers joins the parents' consent, so the gossip the Kural's lover enjoys in fancy becomes one of the voices that brings the marriage about.

links.note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
links.teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

links.note: Kural 447: who can ruin those who keep companions that rebuke them? Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking companions (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்) that it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread past bearing.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the rebuking companion a ruler's best protection; the lover grants the rebuke its good intent and shows where it stops, since love has spread like butter on hot rock before any word could check it, so the ethic of correction meets its limit at kaamam.

links.note: Kural 1199: though the one she longs for gives no grace (நல்கார்), even word of him is sweet to her ears. Kuruntokai 60: even if her lover does not grace her (நல்கார்) or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
links.teaches: Both women claim sweetness from a lover who gives none, with the same verb; Paranar's simile of the cripple licking his empty palm beneath the honeycomb shows what the couplet's maxim hides, that this sweetness is tasted only in imagination, a pleasure that is also the measure of what is withheld.

source_issues: 46 lines 6-7 recur word for word as Kuruntokai 330 lines 6-7 (flagged); marked as written, as a shared closing formula.
48 lines 1-4: the construction is uncertain (who gives the warning about the pollen doll, and whether நினை in line 4 is 'thinking' or 'you'); the verse is marked uncertain.
52 line 5: பரிந்தனென் may be 'I pitied' or 'I pleaded'; the addressee is taken as the girl named in lines 3-4; the verse is marked uncertain.
56 line 5 is the repaired reading of tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), flagged by show; marked as repaired.
The Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (X கூற்று), so every addressee in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and occasion.stage is left null.
